2027-07-11.title: Second Sunday of Kaitha
2027-07-11.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The new covenant of love in the Spirit
The parable of the prodigal son
2027-07-11.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which began on Sunday 4 July: after the apostles have sown the Gospel, the Church looks at its growth and fruit. This is the season of the apostles and martyrs who watered the Church with their blood, and of watchfulness for the coming of the Lord. The Fridays of Kaitha remember martyrs and saints of the East Syriac tradition. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar gives longer forms: Isaiah 3:16–4:6; 2 Corinthians 3:4–18; Luke 15:4–32. In the Latin calendar today is the Fifteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time; St Benedict (11 July) gives way to the Sunday.
2027-07-11.verse: But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion; he ran and put his arms around him and kissed him.
theo: The first reading is part of Moses' last sermon, and it begins with a question that reaches across the whole history of the world: “For ask now about former ages, long before your own, ever since the day that God created human beings on the earth; ask from one end of heaven to the other: has anything so great as this ever happened or has its like ever been heard of?” Moses asks whether any people has ever heard the voice of a god speaking out of a fire and lived, and whether any god has ever gone to take a nation for himself “by trials, by signs and wonders, by war, by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm”, as the Lord did in Egypt. Then the reason is given in one sentence, which the calendar rightly calls the eternal love of God: “And because he loved your ancestors, he chose their descendants after them.” Israel was not chosen because it was great, but because it was loved. The commandments that follow, “for your own well-being and that of your descendants after you”, come after the love, as a father's rule comes after the father's embrace.

In Isaiah the prophet looks beyond a time of judgment: “On that day the branch of the Lord shall be beautiful and glorious.” The Church has always heard in the word Branch the promised king of David's line (compare Jeremiah 23:5), and in the survivors in Zion, “everyone who has been recorded for life in Jerusalem”, the holy people he gathers. God cleanses Jerusalem “by a spirit of judgment and by a spirit of burning”, and then, as in the Exodus, he creates over Mount Zion “a cloud by day and smoke and the shining of a flaming fire by night”. The last verse is a picture for every monsoon in Kerala: over all the glory there will be “a canopy. It will serve as a pavilion, a shade by day from the heat, and a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain.” This is the Church in the season of Kaitha, which begins in the heat and the heavy rains of July: a tent that God himself spreads over his people. (The longer reading begins with the woes on the proud daughters of Zion, and the calendar's heading remembers only the promise.)

Paul's Epistle is about confidence. “Not that we are competent of ourselves to claim anything as coming from us; our competence is from God, who has made us competent to be ministers of a new covenant, not of letter but of spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” He compares the ministry of Moses, whose face shone with a glory that Israel could not bear to look at, with the ministry of the Spirit. Paul does not despise the first: it “came in glory”. He says that when a greater glory appears, the first looks pale beside it, as a lamp beside the sun. This is not a rejection of the Jewish people or their covenant; the Church teaches that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29), and Paul himself was a son of that covenant. His point is that what Jeremiah promised has come: the law written on hearts by the Holy Spirit (Jeremiah 31:33). And so, he says, “we act with great boldness”. The minister of this covenant does not shine by himself; he lets the Spirit give life.

Then comes the Gospel, the most famous of all parables, which the calendar calls the parable of the prodigal son, though it is better called the parable of the father. It is the third of three: a lost sheep, a lost coin, a lost son. St Luke tells us why Jesus told them: the Pharisees and scribes were grumbling, “This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them.” The younger son asks for his share while his father is alive, which is as good as saying, I wish you were dead. He goes to a distant country, spends everything, and ends up feeding pigs, the lowest place a Jewish young man can imagine, wishing he could eat what the pigs eat. Then comes the turning: “when he came to himself.” He rehearses a speech: “I have sinned against heaven and before you.” But before he can say it, the father, who has been watching the road, sees him “while he was still far off”, is “filled with compassion”, runs (an old man does not run in an Eastern village), embraces and kisses him. The robe, the ring and the sandals are the signs of a son, not of a servant; the fatted calf is for a feast. “For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found!”

The parable has a second half, and Jesus meant it for his critics. The elder son, who has stayed, comes in from the field, hears the music, and is angry and will not go in. And the father goes out again, as he went out to the younger, and pleads with him: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But we had to celebrate and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.” The elder son says “this son of yours”; the father answers “this brother of yours”. The parable ends without telling us whether he went in. That is not an accident: the open door is held out to everyone who ever thought of himself as faithful and cannot bear the joy of mercy. Many Kerala families know both sons: one who went to a distant land and came home, and one who stayed and carried the house. Both are loved. The Church answers the father's call in the sacrament of Reconciliation, where the robe is given again, and in the Holy Qurbana, which is the feast of the fatted calf.
conn: “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son” (Hosea 11:1); “I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you” (Jeremiah 31:3).

“The days are surely coming, says the Lord, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land” (Jeremiah 23:5).

“The Lord went in front of them in a pillar of cloud by day, to lead them along the way, and in a pillar of fire by night, to give them light” (Exodus 13:21). “For you have been a refuge to the poor, a refuge to the needy in their distress, a shelter from the rainstorm and a shade from the heat” (Isaiah 25:4).

“I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (Jeremiah 31:33); “for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29).
“As a father has compassion for his children, so the Lord has compassion for those who fear him” (Psalm 103:13).
“Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance” (Luke 15:7).
altar: At every Holy Qurbana the Father runs down the road to meet us. Words of repentance and prayers for forgiveness are said in the Qurbana, and the answer is the table: the robe of the Spirit, the ring of the covenant, and the fatted calf, the Body and Blood of Christ, the feast that the Father makes for those who were lost and are found.

The elder brother is at the altar too, with his questions and his good deeds. The same Lord who gives himself to the sinner comes out to plead with the one who is angry at mercy; he says to each of us: all that is mine is yours. Whoever receives the Qurbana is asked to go into the house and sit at the table with his brother.
outline: A father at the gate, looking down the road.
The eternal love that chooses before it commands; the question of Moses.
The Branch, the holy remnant, and the shelter from the heat and the storm.
The ministry of the new covenant; boldness without pride; the gifts irrevocable.
Lost sheep, lost coin, lost son; the younger son comes to himself, the robe, the ring, the feast.
The father goes out again; this brother of yours; the open door.
“This son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found!”
live: If you have been away from confession or the Qurbana, rehearse a short prayer, ‘Father, I have sinned’, and go this week.
Go out to the elder brother (Luke 15:28)
Is there someone at home or in the parish who is angry about mercy shown to someone else? Go out to them and listen.
Pray every evening for one person who has gone away from the Church, and keep a lamp on in your heart.
Give thanks for the covenant (2 Corinthians 3:6)
Read one page of the Gospel this week and ask the Spirit to write it on your heart.
fathers: You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.

The father saw him from afar and ran, because mercy is quicker than the sinner's footsteps. The robe is the grace that was lost, the ring is the seal of the Spirit, the shoes are the readiness for the Gospel, and the feast is the Body of the Lord.
magis: God chose Israel because he loved it; his love is everlasting and faithful, and Scripture compares it to the love of a father for his child.
The process of conversion and repentance was described by Jesus in the parable of the prodigal son, whose centre is the merciful father.
The Jewish people are the first to hear the Word of God; to them belong the covenants, and the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable.
saints: Second Sunday of Kaitha. In the Latin calendar, the Fifteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time; St Benedict, whose memorial falls on 11 July, gives way to the Sunday.
Mon 12: Second Monday of Kaitha. Thu 15: Sts Kuriakose and Julitta. Fri 16: Our Lady of Mount Carmel and Mar Mari, disciple of Mar Addai.
2027-07-11.prayer: Father of mercies, who chose your people because you loved them, and who watch the road for each of your children, we thank you for your Son, who has told us what you are like. Bring home all who are far away, and give us the courage to say, ‘Father, I have sinned.’ Clothe us again with the robe of your Spirit, put on our hand the ring of your covenant, and seat us at the table of your Son. Teach those of us who have stayed at home to share your joy, and to welcome our brothers and sisters without grudging. Spread over your Church the canopy of your protection against the heat and the storm, and write your law on our hearts. We ask this through Jesus Christ, your Son, who with you and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever. Amen.

quick: Deuteronomy: because the Lord loved your ancestors he chose their descendants; acknowledge today that the Lord is God.
Isaiah: the Branch of the Lord, the holy remnant, and a canopy as a shade by day and a shelter from storm and rain.
Paul: our competence is from God; the new covenant is of the Spirit, who gives life; we act with boldness.
Luke: the father runs to the returning son, and goes out again to plead with the elder one.
2027-07-11.action: Pray each evening this week for one person who has gone away from the faith or from the family, and say to someone at home: ‘I am glad you are here.’
2027-07-11.question: Am I the younger son who needs to return, or the elder who will not come in?
catechism: The covenants and the Jewish people.
Pardon in the sacrament of Penance.
kidsaint: A girl called Rosa was born in 1877 at Kattoor near Thrissur in Kerala. As a young woman she joined the Carmelite sisters who followed Father Chavara, and she took the name Euphrasia. She prayed for hours before Jesus in the tabernacle, especially for people who had gone far from God, so that they might come home like the son in today's Gospel. She died in 1952, and Pope Francis declared her a saint in 2014, together with St Chavara. Lesson: you can bring someone home to God by praying for them every day.
2027-07-11.special: Second Sunday of Kaitha: the father who runs to meet his lost son.
term: A Syriac word meaning ‘my lord’, used as a title of honour for saints and bishops in the Syriac tradition: Mar Thoma, Mar Yakob, Mar Mari, Mar Addai. In the calendar of Kaitha it appears again and again, because this season remembers the saints of the East Syriac Church. Malayalam: മാർ.

family.explain: A boy took his father's money and went far away and spent it all. When he was hungry he decided to go home. Before he even reached the door, his father saw him from far off and ran to meet him and hugged him! The father gave him new clothes and made a big feast. Our heavenly Father is just like that. However far we go, he is watching the road, and he is always glad to see us come home.
family.intention: We pray for people who are far from home, for children who are away at school or work, and for those who have no family.
family.ask: Ask: “When did someone welcome us back after we did something wrong, and how did it feel?”

illus: In a village near Changanassery (a story told to illustrate the reading) an old father kept the front-gate lamp lit every night for ten years, though his younger son had gone to the Gulf and stopped writing. His elder son thought it a waste of oil and said so. ‘He will come back when he is ready,’ said the old man, ‘and I want him to see the light.’ One monsoon evening a thin man in a wet shirt stood at the gate and did not dare to come in. The old man was on the road before the dogs had barked. The elder brother stood at the veranda and could not move. Later that night the old man said to him, ‘Come and sit with us. The house is full tonight, and you are the one who kept it standing.’ The elder son sat down, and the lamp was left lit.

pm.open: Heavenly Father, who run to meet us on the road, gather us in your house, and let us hear your voice saying: you are my son, my daughter. Amen.
share: Because he loved your ancestors, he chose their descendants after them (Deuteronomy 4:37). How has God's love been shown to my family before I was born?
A canopy, a shade by day from the heat, and a refuge from the storm and rain (Isaiah 4:6). Where in my life do I need such a shelter today?
The Spirit gives life (2 Corinthians 3:6). Where am I living by the letter only?
While he was still far off, his father saw him (Luke 15:20). What would I say if I went home to the Father today?
pm.resp: Father, we have sinned; receive us.
interc: For the Church in the season of Kaitha, that she may be a canopy of mercy for all who are in the heat and the storm.
For those who have left the faith or the family, that they may find the way home.
For all who feel unworthy to be called sons and daughters, that they may hear the Father's welcome.
For priests and confessors, that they may be like the father who runs to meet the penitent.
For those of us who have stayed at home, that we may share the joy of the Father.
pm.close: Father, you have made us for yourself. Bring us home, bring home those we love, and seat us all at your table, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today Moses asks Israel: has anything so great as this ever happened? And he gives the answer: God loved your ancestors, and he chose their children after them (Deuteronomy 4:37). Before there is any law, there is love. Before we do anything, we are loved. That is the first message of today.

The prophet Isaiah says that God will spread over his people a canopy, “a shade by day from the heat, and a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain” (Isaiah 4:6). In these July days, when the rain is heavy in Kerala and the sun is hot between the clouds, we know what a good roof means. The Church is that roof, which God himself has put over us.

Saint Paul says that we have a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit: “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). God does not want us only to obey rules. He wants to write his love on our hearts.

And the Gospel gives us the picture of that love, in the father who runs. The younger son asks for his share and goes away and loses everything. But he comes to himself and says, ‘I will go back to my father.’ And before he even finishes his speech, the father sees him far off, is filled with compassion, runs, embraces and kisses him. He gives him the best robe, a ring and sandals and holds a feast. “This son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found!” (Luke 15:24).

But there is also the elder son, who is angry. He has been working faithfully, and he cannot bear the party. The father goes out to him as well: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31). We do not know if he went in. That is the question left for us.

Whether we are the younger or the elder, the Father is waiting at the gate. This week, if you have been far away, go back, and go to confession. If you have stayed, go out and welcome your brother and sister. Let the lamp be lit for those who have not yet come home. Amen.
kids: Children, in today's story a father had two sons. One went away and lost everything, but when he came back the father ran to hug him! God is like that father. If you do something wrong, do not hide. Say sorry and go to him, and he will run to meet you. And if your brother or sister is forgiven, be happy for him or her too, as the father wanted the elder son to be. Let us all come to the party!

intro: Theme: “This son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found!”
On the Second Sunday of Kaitha: the love that chooses before it commands, the canopy over Zion, the Spirit who gives life, and the Father who runs to the younger son and goes out to the elder.

sub: Well-being for you and your descendants.
q: And because he loved your ancestors, he chose their descendants after them.
For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.
points.apply: Thank God this week for one way he loved your family before you were born.

points.h: A canopy against the heat and the storm
sub: Cloud by day and fire by night.
q: It will serve as a pavilion, a shade by day from the heat, and a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain.
See, the home of God is among mortals. He will dwell with them; they will be his peoples, and God himself will be with them;
points.apply: Be a shelter this week for one person in your parish who is in a storm.

q: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
who has made us competent to be ministers of a new covenant, not of letter but of spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
points.apply: Read a page of the Gospel each day and ask the Spirit to write it on your heart.

sub: The younger son comes to himself.
The elder son and the open door.
q: As a father has compassion for his children, so the Lord has compassion for those who fear him.
But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion; he ran and put his arms around him and kissed him.
points.apply: Go to confession, or go out to someone who is angry at mercy.

concl: God chooses because he loves, shelters his people like a canopy, writes his law on their hearts, and runs to meet the one who returns.
Let us go home, and let us open the door to our brothers and sisters.
2027-07-11.resolve: This week, return to the Father, welcome someone home, and pray for those who are still far away.
